blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Instruction-based image editing models can now add, remove a specified number of objects or change their category while preserving the scene. Yet these models often fail to produce the correct number, and these failures grow sharply as scenes become more complex and the requested count increases. Current benchmarks largely miss this problem: they score edits with holistic similarity metrics or with vision-language model (VLM) judges that are themselves poor at counting, so numerical errors go unnoticed or are graded incorrectly. As a result, the true numerical ability of today's editing models has never been accurately measured. We address this issue with ABACUS, a new benchmark, evaluation protocol and dedicated scoring metric for numerical image editing. Our protocol is judge-free: no VLM or MLLM scores an edit or counts objects (a VLM only confirms the category of rare ambiguous crops). Instead, it verifies each edit at the instance level against panoptic ground truth confirmed by detector consensus, checking both that the exact requested count was achieved and that the rest of the scene was preserved, across the add, remove and change operations. By evaluating leading image editors, our method reveals substantial numerical editing failures that worsen with increasing scene complexity and object count; failures that prior benchmarks often overlooked or misjudged.
blocks.zh: 基于指令的图像编辑模型现在可以在保留场景的同时添加,删除指定数量的对象或更改其类别. 然而,这些模型往往不能产生正确的数字,这些失败随着场景变得更加复杂和要求的计数增加而急剧增加. 目前的基准在很大程度上忽略了这个问题:它们用整体相似性衡量标准或视觉语言模型(VLM)评分,这些评分本身在计数上很差,所以数字误差不被注意或分级错误. 因此,今天的编辑模型的真实数值能力从未被精确地测量. 我们用ABACUS来处理这个问题,这是一个新的基准、评价协议和数字图像编辑专用评分指标。 我们的协议是无判断的:没有VLM或MLLM评分一个编辑或计数对象(一个VLM只确认罕见的模棱两可的作物类别). 相反,它根据探测器协商一致确认的全光学地面真实性,在实例一级核实每一次编辑,同时检查所要求准确的计数是否已经实现,以及现场的其余部分是否得到保存,在整个添加,移除和更改操作. 通过评价主要图像编辑器,我们的方法揭示出大量的数值编辑失败,随着场景的日益复杂和对象的计数而恶化;先前的基准常常忽略或误判的失败.

blocks.en:
Instruction-based image editing has advanced rapidly: a single model can
now add, remove, or change objects in a real image from a short
natural-language command. Proprietary systems such as Gemini 2.5 Flash
Image (“Nano Banana”) [ 12 ] , Seedream 4.0 [ 36 ] ,
and GPT-Image-1 [ 27 ] , together with strong open models such as
Qwen-Image-Edit [ 40 ] , FLUX.1 Kontext [ 4 ] ,
Step1X-Edit [ 24 ] , and BAGEL [ 10 ] , produce edits that
are visually convincing and, at a glance, faithful to the instruction.
However, producing the exact number of objects an instruction
requests ( numerical editing), as in “add three boats”, “remove
two cars”, or “change four of the cows into sheep”, is quite hard.
The model must produce the right count, and it must do so without disturbing the rest of the scene : it should not silently add
an unrequested object, delete an existing one, or repurpose an original
instance to fake the count. We find that editors frequently fail at this
(Fig. 1 ), and that the failures grow sharply as scenes become more crowded and
the requested count increases, precisely the regime where reliable counting
matters most.

Measuring this matters beyond the editor. Generative editing is increasingly
used to build controlled training data [ 46 , 16 ] : when real
images of a configuration are scarce (rare counts, dense crowds, long-tail
categories), an editor renders a set number of instances, and one silent
miscount corrupts every downstream label. Being judge-free, deterministic, and
grounded in detected evidence, the same signal could also serve as a verifiable
reward (RLVR) for post-training editors toward exact counting, where a learned
VLM reward would be noisy and reward-hackable.

The deeper problem is that we cannot currently measure this failure :
the instruments used to evaluate editing are themselves unreliable for
counting (Sec. 2 ). Holistic similarity metrics
(CLIP [ 33 ] , DINO [ 7 ] , L 1 / L 2 L_{1}/L_{2} , FID [ 15 ] ), as in
MagicBrush [ 45 ] , capture global appearance but are blind to
instance counts. The now-dominant alternative scores edits with a VLM or MLLM judge [ 19 , 25 , 42 , 41 , 31 , 17 ] ,
which is circular: VLMs are themselves poor counters. Their accuracy collapses
with object number and variety [ 13 , 35 , 3 , 14 ] ,
they miss small edits [ 19 , 22 ] , score
unreliably [ 29 , 20 ] , and have no notion of instance correspondence : when a model turns one of two people into a
third, or deletes the sources and paints the targets elsewhere, the judge
still reports success (Fig. 1 ). Editors’ numerical ability
has thus been overlooked or misjudged.

blocks.en:
We argue that numerical editing must be verified , not judged. We
introduce ABACUS, a benchmark, an evaluation protocol, and a dedicated
scoring metric for numerical image editing. ABACUS is built on COCO
images [ 21 ] with high-quality panoptic ground truth from
COCONut [ 11 ] , and it scores every edit by reconstructing what happened to each object instance rather than by asking a model
for an opinion. It segments every instance in both images [ 6 ] ,
matches before/after instances with a matcher robust to generative appearance
drift, and confirms each category by the independent agreement of two
detectors [ 34 , 47 ] . From this, it assigns every object a verdict
( kept , added , removed , transformed ) and jointly
checks the exact requested count and scene conservation across
add, remove, and change. No VLM or MLLM ever judges an edit or counts objects.

blocks.en: 2.2 Benchmarks and metrics for image editing
blocks.zh: 2.2 图像编辑的基准和衡量标准

blocks.en:
Early evaluation relied on holistic similarity metrics (CLIP [ 33 ] , DINO [ 7 ] , L 1 L_{1} ,
FID [ 15 ] ), as used to score MagicBrush [ 45 ] edits, which are
insensitive to object count. The field has since moved to VLM/MLLM judges . VIEScore [ 19 ] prompts an MLLM for an explainable
score but correlates only weakly with humans and is itself noted to miss
small edits. I2EBench [ 25 ] , ImgEdit-Bench [ 42 ] ,
KRIS-Bench [ 41 ] , and CompBench [ 17 ] score edits
across many dimensions with MLLM judges. Notably, I2EBench and KRIS-Bench
even include a dedicated counting dimension, yet they grade it with a VLM
(GPT-4V / GPT-4o), inheriting exactly the counting unreliability we
document. GEdit-Bench [ 24 ] grades against real-world
instructions. RefEdit [ 30 ] contributes
RefEdit-Bench (rooted in RefCOCO) for referring-expression edits and reports
that editors handling a single prominent object degrade sharply once a scene
contains multiple entities, reinforcing our focus on scene complexity. And
learned scorers such as ADIEE [ 8 ] and human-aligned MLLM
judges [ 22 ] try to repair judge reliability. All keep a model in the scoring loop for a task
that model performs poorly, and none target exact count with
instance correspondence. Two efforts move toward grounding.
GIE-Bench [ 31 ] adds object-aware conservation masks but still
verifies functional correctness with VLM-answered multiple-choice
questions. EdiVal-Agent [ 9 ] is the closest in spirit: it is
object-centric and reports that detectors combined with a VLM agree with
humans better than a VLM alone, which corroborates our premise. It differs
from ABACUS in both goal and mechanism. EdiVal-Agent measures multi-turn instruction following : for symbolic edit types, including a
count-change task, it scores with a single open-vocabulary detector, but for
semantic types it routes detector-localized crops to a VLM and it generates
its instructions and object pool with a VLM, so the framework is judge-based
overall. Notably, its counts are read from one detector on arbitrary
images with no verified ground-truth reference. ABACUS instead targets exact-count fidelity and scene conservation , grounding every verdict in
panoptic ground truth, segmentation, geometric matching, and two-detector
agreement, and never asking a VLM to count objects or judge whether an edit succeeded. Uniquely, it repairs
incomplete ground truth and checks that a “change” transformed the same instances in place . Table 1(a) summarizes this positioning: no prior benchmark provides a fully
judge-free, instance-level protocol that jointly verifies exact count and
conservation, which is the gap ABACUS fills.

blocks.en:
Concretely, ABACUS grounds counting in detection and segmentation. We build on
COCO [ 21 ] with COCONut panoptic masks [ 11 ] , which are strong
enough to anchor instance-level verification while our pipeline is built to
tolerate their residual faults, and on strong detectors [ 34 , 47 ] whose occasional errors are absorbed downstream by detector agreement,
presence-gated segmentation [ 6 ] , and the matching and
ground-truth-completion steps. The resulting verdicts are verifiable rather
than opined.

The ground-truth counts come from panoptic annotation confirmed by the

blocks.en: 3.2 Operations, difficulty, and scene complexity
blocks.zh: 3.2 操作、困难和场景复杂

blocks.en:
ABACUS covers three operations: adding K K objects of a category, removing K K of them, and changing K K instances of one category into another (one
example of each in Fig. S5 of App. A ). Rather than bin
difficulty by a single attribute, we grade it
with a composite
score built from three complementary axes, each rank-normalized to [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] over the pool: the foreground coverage of the scene (fraction of
pixels that are foreground), the target count (the maximum number of
target instances the scene admits, which bounds the requested K K ), and the target-object scale (the share of the foreground occupied by the
target category, target-class pixels over foreground pixels, where a smaller
share is harder). Their sum gives a difficulty score in [ 0 , 3 ] [0,3] that we
split at its terciles into easy, medium, and hard tiers
(examples in Fig. S6 of App. A ). The split is meaningful rather than arbitrary,
and non-circular: scene attributes that do not enter the score (the
number of instances, the number of categories, and the crowd ratio) still
separate the tiers, and model performance decreases monotonically across them
(Sec. 5.3 and Table 2 ; validated in App. A ). Overall, ABACUS comprises 10,944 10{,}944 instructions over 3,845 3{,}845 COCO images, roughly balanced across the three tiers and the add, remove, and change operations (Table 1(b) ).

Clean-image construction. To count only what was added, we remove the preserved scene: the matched
(existing) regions are erased from I e I_{e} with classical Non-Local Patch-Based
inpainting [ 26 ] , a non-generative fill that introduces no new
content, and the genuine-new regions are composited back to form a clean edited image that ideally contains the additions alone.
Isolating the new content this way lets a new object be counted even when it
sits in front of or overlaps a pre-existing one.

这样孤立新内容, 即使新对象被计算在内

blocks.en:

clean image and vote independently on the SAM-localized regions: for
each genuine-new mask, each detector is asked only whether a cls \mathrm{cls} box
overlaps that region, and the mask is confirmed when both agree.
Decoupling the vote (each detector agrees with the SAM region, not with the
other detector’s exact box) recovers objects that both see but box slightly
differently, while the two-detector gate still blocks single-detector false
positives. Masks that resolve to the same detector box are re-anchored to a
single instance, and a standard cross-detector consensus catches objects SAM
missed entirely.

Annotating this set by hand is not a convenience but a necessity. Image
editing models still fail to produce the requested number of objects,
and the gap widens as the count and scene complexity
grow [ 30 , 3 , 14 ] ; on our set the number of
target objects actually present in an edited image rarely equals the
prompt’s target K K . The prompt count K K is therefore a property of the instruction , not of the image: using it as the reference would
conflate the editor’s failure with the evaluator’s, and reward an evaluator
for parroting K K rather than for counting what is on the canvas. We instead
annotate the true number of target-category objects in each edited image and
validate every evaluator against this human count, never against K K .

Table 2 reports the main result: leading editors miss the
requested count on most edits, especially for remove and change and in cluttered scenes. Decomposing the score exposes two
compounding failures: count fidelity (CF) is the weakest factor, and
original-category conservation (OC) is also low, as editors frequently
overwrite or delete existing same-category objects when adding, and
spuriously insert new ones when removing.
Only scene consistency (SC) stays high, so the surrounding background is
preserved even when the target objects are not. The proprietary systems lead
the open models by a clear margin, yet even the strongest, Seedream 4.0,
reaches only 0.31 0.31 overall. Because the Score multiplies three factors,
even the best system fails at least one of count, conservation, or scene
preservation on most edits.

blocks.en: 5.4 Ablations

blocks.en:
We ablate each component on the 600 human-annotated images of
Sec. 5.1 , removing one at a time and re-measuring exact-count
agreement against the human count
(Table S3 of App. C.2 ). Each part is load-bearing, but to different

(0.82 to 0.36): instead of re-matching every source instance to its
drifted counterpart in the edit, the source mask is reused in place ,
and the editor’s small shifts in position and size leave it covering nothing,
so the preserved object is never masked out and is recounted as new. The next
three each cost about ten points: clean-image isolation inpaints the matched
objects out, and without it the detectors count pre-existing and added
instances together; ground-truth completion guards the opposite error,
rescuing a real object the incomplete panoptic labels would otherwise score as
new; and a single detector (averaged over keeping only RF-DETR or only
Co-DETR) admits class false positives that the dual-detector agreement filters.
The constrained VLM verifier matters least (0.82 to 0.79): it only
confirms a category on the rare ambiguous crop, so ABACUS’s accuracy rests on
grounded geometry and detection, not the VLM, and the protocol stays
judge-free.

blocks.en: 6 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 6 结论

blocks.en:
We argued that numerical image editing must be verified , not judged,
and proposed ABACUS, which combines three components: a numerically
controlled benchmark with instance-level ground truth, a judge-free evaluation
protocol, and a scoring metric that jointly rewards the exact requested count
and the conservation of the rest of the scene. ABACUS matches human counting
where VLMs and single detectors collapse, and benchmarking leading editors
reveals a failure the field had overlooked: even the strongest systems still cannot count, delivering the wrong number of
objects on most edits, or reaching the target only by overwriting what was
already there.
blocks.zh:
我们主张,数字图像编辑必须经过核实,而不是判断,
和拟议的ABACUS,它包括三个组成部分:

现场忽略了一个失败:即使最强大的系统也仍然无法计算,交付错误的数目
对象在大多数编辑上,或只通过覆盖什么来达到目标
已经在这里了。

blocks.en:
Scope and limitations. ABACUS is scoped to the 80 80 COCO
thing-categories by design: reliable judge-free confirmation needs a fixed
detector vocabulary, and outside it, the closed-set detectors return no
detections. Extending to rarer categories needs open-vocabulary detectors,
themselves less reliable for counting (the failure ABACUS avoids). Open-vocabulary
numerical editing is the natural next step. Extending it to other domains
and detectors (e.g., aerial imagery) is a further direction. ABACUS also scores the count and
scene conservation, not which specific instances are chosen: any valid K K -subset satisfies the instruction when K < N K\!<\!N , while conservation still
blocks reaching the count by replacing existing ones. Numerical edits with attribute and positioning constraints, which instances to edit and with which attributes, are the next research axes.

blocks.en:
Our difficulty tiers are not hand-set thresholds but a reproducible,
data-driven construction that we then independently validate. Each
{image, category} pair is graded on three complementary axes
(Sec. 3.2 ): scene occupancy (foreground ratio, ↑ \uparrow harder), target visibility (target-to-foreground ratio, ↓ \downarrow harder), and edit capacity (maximum addable count, ↑ \uparrow harder). Because the raw axes live on incomparable scales, we
rank-normalize each to a near-uniform [ 0 , 1 ] [0,1] score, sum them into a composite
difficulty in [ 0 , 3 ] [0,3] , and split at its terciles into easy/medium/hard
(cut-points 1.27 1.27 and 1.73 1.73 ; observed scores span 0.08 0.08 – 2.94 2.94 ). The
split is thus balanced by construction, with no arbitrary cut-offs.

blocks.en: B.3 Repairing incomplete ground truth
blocks.zh: B.3 修复不完整的地面真相

blocks.en:
The panoptic annotations are strong but not perfect: some instances are simply
not labelled. A naive pipeline would then count a real, pre-existing object as newly added , inflating the realized count. ABACUS guards against this by
segmenting the source image as well, not just the edit: every candidate
flagged as new is cross-checked against the source segmentation, and if a
confident counterpart is present in the original it is reassigned to existing (“rescued”) rather than counted as new
(Sec. 4.1 ). Figure S12 shows a clear case on an
“add 2 chairs” edit: the chairs in the background were present in the original
but missing from the annotation, so SAM-3 first marks them as new; the
source-image cross-check finds their counterparts and rescues them, so only the
genuinely added chairs are counted.

blocks.en: B.4 Matching under generative drift
blocks.zh: B.4 基因漂移下的匹配

blocks.en:
Figure S14 shows why exact-count editing needs more than a direct
judge. The edit inserts two cars so naturally that the before/after pair looks
like an ordinary street: a VLM judge sees a plausible result and cannot say
what, or how much, changed. ABACUS’s geometry-and-appearance matcher
(Sec. 4.1 ) instead places every edited instance against the source.
It confirms the pre-existing car as matched (e1) and flags the two
inserted cars as genuinely new (e0 and e2, with high segmentation
scores), recovering the exact added count that a direct judge would miss.

blocks.en:
To produce each edited image, we query the editor with the benchmark
instruction (Sec. 3.1 ) followed by a fixed
scene-preservation suffix that asks the model to alter only the requested
objects. For addition, the full prompt is: “Add K K { category } to the scene. Keep everything else exactly as-is: same
background, lighting, colors, composition, and camera angle. Do not alter, move,
or remove existing objects. Only add the new element in a realistic,
naturally-placed position.” Removal and change use the analogous instruction with a matching preservation
suffix. Holding this suffix fixed across all editors keeps the comparison fair:
every model is explicitly asked to preserve the rest of the scene, so a low
original-category conservation score reflects the editor’s behaviour, not a
difference in prompting.

Intended uses. ABACUS is intended for evaluating numerical
image editing. Because its score is deterministic, grounded, and judge-free, it
could also serve as a verifiable reward for training editors toward exact
counting, or as a filter for count-controlled data generation; we have not
tested these uses and leave them to future work.
